title: Adult Sleep Hours Calculator 2026 | Hacé Cuentas
h1: How Much Sleep Do Adults Need by Age?
description: AASM/NSF guidelines: young adults 18-25 and adults 26-64 need 7-9 hours; adults 65+ need 7-8 hours. Evidence-based calculator from US sleep medicine standards.
intro: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) and the National Sleep Foundation (NSF) publish the consensus sleep duration recommendations used by US clinicians: young adults 18-25 years and adults 26-64 years should obtain 7-9 hours of sleep per night, while older adults 65 and over should target 7-8 hours. These ranges come from a joint AASM/Sleep Research Society expert panel that reviewed over 5,000 studies linking sleep duration to cardiometabolic, immune, and cognitive outcomes. The most recent CDC Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance data (2022) show US adults averaging a median of 7.0 hours, but roughly 35% of adults report habitually sleeping fewer than 7 hours — the threshold the CDC officially classifies as short sleep and a public health epidemic. Individual variation does exist: carriers of the rare DEC2 (BHLHE41) and ADRB1 short-sleeper gene variants can function on 4-6 hours without measurable impairment, but these mutations affect well under 1% of the population, so assuming you are one of them is statistically unwise. Sleep debt is cumulative — chronic restriction does not produce adaptation, only normalization of impaired performance.
keyTakeaway: **AASM/NSF recommendations: Young adults (18-25) and adults (26-64) need 7-9 hours nightly. Older adults (65+) need 7-8 hours.** Sub-7-hour sleep is associated with cardiovascular, metabolic, and cognitive risk in over 99% of the population.

seoKeywords: how much sleep do adults need
explanation:
## Sleep Architecture and Why Duration Matters

A normal night of sleep is organized into 4-6 ninety-minute cycles, each containing the four stages defined by the AASM scoring manual. Stage N1 (transitional light sleep) occupies roughly 5% of the night, N2 (the bulk of light sleep, with K-complexes and sleep spindles) makes up about 50%, N3 slow-wave or deep sleep takes 15-25%, and REM sleep accounts for 20-25%. Deep N3 sleep is when glymphatic clearance peaks, growth hormone is secreted, and procedural memory consolidates. REM sleep is when emotional regulation, creative problem solving, and declarative memory are processed. Cutting total sleep time by even 90 minutes — one full cycle — disproportionately removes the REM-heavy cycles that cluster in the second half of the night.

## How Sleep Changes with Age

From the 30s onward, total slow-wave (N3) sleep declines steadily — by age 60 it may be half of what it was at 25. REM percentage stays relatively stable, but sleep becomes more fragmented: more awakenings, lighter mean depth, and earlier morning rise time as the circadian rhythm phase-advances. This is why older adults often need 7-8 hours rather than 7-9, and why sleep efficiency (time asleep ÷ time in bed) drops from 95% in young adults to 80-85% in healthy 70-year-olds. Older adults still need adequate sleep — they just consolidate it less efficiently.

## Insomnia, CBT-i, and the Sleep Hygiene Baseline

The DSM-5 defines insomnia disorder as difficulty initiating or maintaining sleep, or early-morning awakening, occurring at least 3 nights per week for at least 3 months, with clinically significant daytime impact. The AASM clinical practice guideline names cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-i) — not pharmacotherapy — as first-line treatment. CBT-i combines sleep restriction therapy, stimulus control, cognitive restructuring, and sleep hygiene. Sleep hygiene alone is not a treatment for clinical insomnia, but it is the non-negotiable baseline: a consistent sleep and wake schedule (within ±30 minutes daily, weekends included), a bedroom kept dark and cool (65-68°F is the consensus thermoneutral range), no caffeine after 2 p.m. (half-life is approximately 5 hours, so a 3 p.m. coffee still has 25% on board at 1 a.m.), alcohol avoidance in the 3-4 hours before bed because it fragments REM and worsens sleep apnea, and limiting blue-spectrum light exposure in the last hour before bed because evening blue light suppresses melatonin secretion by 50-90%. Vigorous exercise should generally end at least 4 hours before bedtime to allow core body temperature to fall.

## Shift Work, Social Jet Lag, and Catch-Up Myths

Shift workers experience shift work disorder, a circadian misalignment condition with a roughly 2-fold increased risk of obesity, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular events. Social jet lag — the phase shift between weekday and weekend schedules — operates by the same mechanism in non-shift workers. The Tasali 2022 trial (JAMA Internal Medicine) showed that extending habitual sleep duration meaningfully reduced caloric intake, but other work in Diabetes Care has shown that weekend recovery sleep does not fully reverse weekday-restriction-induced insulin resistance. Sleep debt cannot be paid back over one weekend; the metabolic damage requires sustained correction.

## Wearables: Useful, Not Diagnostic

Consumer trackers (Oura, Whoop, Apple Watch, Fitbit) use actigraphy plus heart rate and HRV as proxies. Compared against gold-standard polysomnography, current-generation devices show roughly 86% agreement on total sleep time but consistently overestimate REM and underestimate awakenings during fragmented nights. They are excellent for trend tracking and behavior change; they are not diagnostic for sleep apnea, periodic limb movement disorder, or REM behavior disorder. CGMs add a useful glycemic-stability signal that correlates with sleep quality.

## Cognitive and Long-Term Health Cost

The Williamson and Feyer (2000) study established that 17-19 hours awake produces psychomotor impairment equivalent to a blood alcohol concentration of 0.05%, and 24 hours awake roughly equals BAC 0.10 — above the US legal driving limit of 0.08. Beyond the acute cost, chronic sleep below 6 hours is linked to a 48% increased risk of coronary heart disease, a 30% increased risk of type 2 diabetes, and accelerated beta-amyloid accumulation associated with Alzheimer's disease. Hitting your age-appropriate target is one of the highest-leverage interventions in preventive medicine.

faq.q: How many hours of sleep do I actually need?
faq.a: If you are 18-64, the AASM/NSF target is 7-9 hours per night. If you are 65 or older, the target is 7-8 hours. The most reliable individual signal is whether you wake without an alarm feeling rested and stay alert through the afternoon without caffeine — if not, you are almost certainly under-sleeping.

Eight hours is a useful midpoint of the 7-9 hour recommended range, not a magic number. The evidence supports a range because population studies show a U-shaped mortality curve: risk rises below 7 hours and also above 9 hours in adults. For most US adults, anything inside 7-9 hours is fine.

faq.q: Can I catch up on sleep over the weekend?
faq.a: Partially, and not enough. Recovery sleep restores some cognitive performance, but Diabetes Care studies show weekend catch-up does not reverse the insulin resistance, inflammation, and circadian disruption caused by chronic weekday restriction. Treat 7-9 hours as a daily requirement, not a weekly average.

faq.q: How do I find a CBT-i provider in the US?
faq.a: The Society of Behavioral Sleep Medicine maintains a provider directory at behavioralsleep.org. Many insurance plans cover CBT-i, and FDA-cleared digital programs (Somryst, Sleepio) deliver the protocol via app with documented efficacy comparable to in-person therapy. Your primary care provider can refer you to either.

Melatonin is best used as a circadian phase shifter at low doses (0.3-0.5 mg, 3-5 hours before desired bedtime), not as a sleeping pill. The AASM does not recommend chronic melatonin for primary insomnia, and US-market supplements have been shown to contain anywhere from 17% to 478% of labeled dose. For shift work and jet lag, short-term use is reasonable; for chronic insomnia, CBT-i is the standard of care.

faq.q: Do older adults really need less sleep?
faq.a: Only slightly. The 65+ recommendation is 7-8 hours versus 7-9 for younger adults. What changes more is sleep architecture: less deep sleep, more fragmentation, earlier wake time. If you are over 65 and consistently sleeping under 6 hours, that is short sleep regardless of age and warrants evaluation for sleep apnea, depression, or medication side effects.

For total sleep time, current consumer wearables agree with polysomnography about 86% of the time, which is good enough for trend tracking. They consistently overestimate REM percentage and underestimate brief awakenings. Do not use a tracker to diagnose a sleep disorder — if you suspect sleep apnea, restless legs, or REM behavior disorder, request a home sleep test or in-lab polysomnogram through a board-certified sleep medicine physician.

faq.q: How fast does sleep deprivation impair me?
faq.a: Williamson and Feyer (2000) showed 17-19 hours of continuous wakefulness produces psychomotor impairment equivalent to a blood alcohol level of 0.05%, and 24 hours awake is roughly equivalent to BAC 0.10 — above the US legal driving limit. Driving on under 5 hours of sleep roughly quadruples crash risk relative to 7+ hours.

faq.q: What temperature should my bedroom be?
faq.a: The consensus thermoneutral range for adult sleep is 65-68°F (18-20°C). Core body temperature drops about 1°F across the night as part of normal sleep physiology; a warm bedroom blocks this drop and fragments sleep. Cooler is generally better than warmer.
